notes: DATUM BREAK: USGS Water-Supply Paper 1309 says the recorder datum was lowered 4.24 ft to the present datum on 1934-10-01; before that (chain gauge to 1928-10-17, then the recorder) readings were on a datum 4.24 ft higher. The daily values are not adjusted: yearly minimums jump from -2.9 ft in 1934 to +2.4 ft in 1935. Also April 1936 to September 1937 used mostly a wire-weight gauge at a datum 0.47 ft lower. Do not compare levels across 1934 without adding 4.24 ft to the earlier values (we leave them as published).

Flow has been regulated by Garrison Dam (Lake Sakakawea), about 75 miles upstream, since November 1953. Lake Oahe begins downstream; whether its backwater reaches the gauge was not found in USGS reports.
USGS approval codes in the file: {'A': 45406, 'P': 335, 'A:e': 14}. A (approved) -> measured, P (provisional) -> provisional, any code with 'e' (estimated by USGS) -> estimated, even if approved.
Non-numeric value codes skipped (equipment, ice and similar): none. Dropped 0 fill values.
Daily mean of the gauge's readings for the day, as computed by USGS. In early years the 'daily mean' may rest on one or two staff-gauge readings a day; see measurement_history.
Legacy waterservices.usgs.gov endpoint; USGS plans to retire it in favor of api.waterdata.usgs.gov, so this URL may need to change.
USGS station name: MISSOURI RIVER AT BISMARCK, ND.

measurement_history.fact: Missouri River Commission gauge heights near Bismarck exist for part of the 1880s and May 1886 to December 1899 (exact first dates unclear in scan).
Highest known stage, 31.6 ft at present site and datum, Mar. 31, 1881, from an ice jam.
Weather Bureau gauge-height records near Bismarck begin in June 1891.
USGS says the Bismarck gaging station was established in 1927.
Before Oct. 17, 1928, a chain gauge 2,100 ft upstream at a datum 4.24 ft higher; then a recorder at the present site.
Recorder datum lowered 4.24 ft to the present datum on Oct. 1, 1934.
Apr. 1936 to Sept. 1937, mostly a wire-weight gauge 2,000 ft downstream at a datum 0.47 ft lower.
USGS: flow regulated by Lake Sakakawea (Garrison Dam), 75 miles upstream, since November 1953.
Highest stage before Garrison Dam was 27.90 ft; highest since was 14.58 ft in Dec. 1979, from ice backwater.
Gauge zero 1,618.28 ft above NGVD29 (revised); 1950 report gave 1,618.38 ft. NWS now lists 1,619.46 ft NAVD88.
USACE sets Garrison releases low before the river freezes at Bismarck, then raises them, to manage ice.
Lake Oahe backwater effect on the Bismarck gauge: not found in USGS reports or NWS gauge data checked.

public_notes: Before October 1, 1934, the readings in this file were measured from a gauge zero 4.24 feet higher than today's, and USGS did not adjust them, so early low readings look about 4 feet lower than they would today. Since Garrison Dam began holding back water in 1953, the river here has been lower and steadier, and winter ice can push readings up.
